name: Multidirectional cranial distraction

card.summary: A craniofacial surgery technique that gradually reshapes the skull in several directions using internal distractor devices, correcting head shape and enlarging skull volume.
card.aka: Cranial DO; multidirectional cranial distraction osteogenesis (MCDO)
card.note: Major neurosurgical procedure developed for children with craniosynostosis; performed only by craniofacial teams.

quick.overview:
Multidirectional cranial distraction osteogenesis (MCDO) is a surgical method in which skull bone is cut into segments and then slowly moved apart by implanted devices, so new bone forms in the gaps. Its payoff for appearance is a reshaped head: it is used to correct skull deformities such as those seen in craniosynostosis, where sutures fuse early and distort head shape.

Surgeons describe it as flexible enough to reshape all types of skull deformity in suitable patients, and published case series of children report good outcomes. It sits in the hardmaxx corner of looksmaxxing discussion as an example of how far skull shape can be altered surgically, but its documented use is medical and paediatric.
quick.how: In practice the procedure is done in a hospital by a craniofacial or neurosurgical team. The skull bone is cut, small internal devices are fitted, and after a short waiting period they are activated gradually over weeks, followed by a consolidation period while the bone heals. A later, smaller operation removes the devices. Timing and device choice are planned around the patient's age and deformity.
quick.risks: It is major surgery on the skull. Reported problems with cranial distraction in general include device breakage, infection and bone not forming as intended, and the research literature is overwhelmingly about children with a diagnosed medical condition rather than cosmetic patients. Individual risk depends on age, anatomy and the surgical team, so any decision belongs with a craniofacial specialist.

lead: Multidirectional cranial distraction osteogenesis (MCDO) is a form of distraction osteogenesis applied to the skull. Surgeons cut the cranial vault into pieces and attach distractor devices that slowly pull the pieces apart, letting new bone fill the gaps and the skull expand and change shape in more than one direction at once [4][7].

Its purpose in the literature is to correct deformities of head shape and volume, chiefly in craniosynostosis, the early fusion of skull sutures [1][2]. A Korean neurosurgical group that developed the approach reported that it can reshape all phenotypes of skull deformity except in infants of five months or younger and in posterior vault problems, and described benefits such as flexibility of reshaping, a shorter treatment period and less invasive follow-up surgery [4].

The technique is documented as a medical procedure for children rather than a cosmetic service. It appears in looksmaxxing discussion as part of the hardmaxx vocabulary of skeletal change, where its appearance payoff is a corrected head contour.

chain: Skull cut into segments and fitted with distractors
Segments slowly moved apart; new bone fills the gap
Skull volume and contour reshaped in several directions
angle.text: The procedure changes skull contour directly by growing new bone between repositioned segments. The published use is correction of craniosynostosis deformity, where improved head shape is a core outcome alongside skull volume.

paras: Distraction osteogenesis is a general surgical principle in which bone is cut and the two sides are moved apart very gradually, so the body fills the gap with new bone. It proceeds through osteotomy, a latency period, active distraction at roughly a millimetre a day, and consolidation, after which the device is removed in a second operation [10].

Cranial versions place the distractors on the skull vault. Posterior cranial distraction, a related approach, aims to expand the back of the skull with little dissection of the brain's covering, and a systematic review of 18 articles covering 325 patients found a mean distraction of 24.7 mm and a mean intracranial volume gain of about 253 cm3, with most patients having a syndrome [3].
Multidirectional cranial distraction extends this idea by using devices that act in more than one direction, which the developing group argues allows greater flexibility in reshaping [4].

Craniosynostosis is the premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures; it produces characteristic head shapes and, untreated, can raise intracranial pressure [1][2]. Surgical options include open vault reconstruction, strip craniectomy with a molding helmet or springs, endoscopic release and cranial distraction [1][2].

Case series describe MCDO for bicoronal synostosis and for multiple-suture disease [8][5]. A Korean report of 36 children treated between 2005 and 2014 presented the method as one that can be adapted to different deformities [4]. Distraction has also been reported in rickets-associated sagittal synostosis, where two children achieved 30 mm of transverse distraction and improved cranial proportions maintained at follow-up [5].

General reviews of distraction osteogenesis report infection, bone failing to grow in the intended direction and hardware failure among complications [10]. Cranial distractor breakage has its own reported literature in children with craniosynostosis [9]. The posterior distraction review specifically set out to determine complication rates and the most common complications of that technique [3].

Published human data consist of surgical case series and reviews in children with craniosynostosis, not trials in cosmetic patients. The Korean MCDO series reports 36 children [4], and a 2010 report in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery describes the approach [6]. A systematic review of posterior cranial distraction analysed 325 patients [3]. No studies in healthy adults seeking appearance change were found.

The procedure is not a mainstream topic in looksmaxxing forums; it surfaces mainly as a research curiosity within discussions of hardmaxxing, the category of surgical and skeletal change. The medical literature it rests on concerns children and a diagnosed condition.

timeline.event: Langenbeck proposes the bone-lengthening principle later called distraction osteogenesis [10].
Ilizarov begins the studies that established distraction osteogenesis in wide use [10].
Korean group treats 36 children with multidirectional cranial distraction [4].
Multidirectional cranial distraction for craniosynostosis described in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery [6].
Review introduces MCDO as an update to distraction osteogenesis [4].
